description: LUNATHEGOAT builds LUNARSEYE for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge: a web tool that uses NASA LOLA terrain and SPICE geometry to compute terrain-aware sunlight and Earth line of sight for 27 south-pole candidate sites, then recommends one site for a mission's needs, with the source of every number. Live: lunarseye.onrender.com. Team of two: frontend + research, backend + algorithm.
summary:
LUNARSEYE is a web tool for comparing lunar south-pole sites for power and communication, built only on NASA data. Pick one of 27 cited candidate sites (NASA PGDA product 78) and it shows the Moon lit from the SPICE Sun direction, the Sun and Earth elevation over a year of hourly samples, and how much of each disc clears the terrain skyline built from the LOLA elevation model. Terrain, Illumination & Earth and Compare pages give slope and roughness from the 20 m LOLA DEM and a side-by-side table.

It addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by answering what a mission planner needs to ask: which sites get sunlight, when Earth is in line of sight, and how steep and rough the ground is. Every number carries an evidence tag (OBS, DERIVED, MODEL, CALC, ASSUMED, PLACEHOLDER or N/C) that opens its source, method, limits and SHA-256, so nothing looks more certain than it is. It is a preliminary research tool, not a certified landing system.
details:
What it does: LUNARSEYE compares candidate lunar south-pole sites on the two things a lander needs, sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for communication. Pick one of 27 cited sites (tile centres from NASA PGDA product 78, Barker et al. 2021, not landing points) from the list or the 3D Moon. The Overview page shows the Moon lit from the SPICE Sun direction and, for a full year of hourly samples (2027), the Sun and Earth elevation against the terrain horizon at that site, the visible fraction of each disc, time in sunlight, longest darkness, time with Earth in view and longest Earth outage. The Illumination & Earth page shows the sky and horizon at the site, the Terrain page shows height, slope and roughness from the 20 m LOLA DEM plus a 3D south-pole terrain view, Compare puts sites side by side, and Data lists every dataset with its source and SHA-256.

How it works: Sun and Earth positions come from NAIF SPICE (DE440s, MOON_ME frame). A terrain horizon of 1440 azimuths out to 200 km, corrected for curvature, is built from LOLA LDEM_75S_240M with the observer 2 m above the surface (a stated assumption). Sunlight and Earth line of sight are the visible disc fraction above that terrain horizon and, separately, above a flat horizon, so the effect of terrain is visible. Slope and roughness are measured over a stated baseline from a window of the 20 m PGDA DEM LDEM_80S_20MPP_ADJ read over HTTP byte ranges (the 2.7 GB file is never downloaded whole). Earth visibility is geometric line of sight only, not a radio link.

Why it matters and what is creative: the numbers that decide a site usually sit in separate datasets and tools. Here every value is tagged OBS / DERIVED / MODEL / CALC / ASSUMED / PLACEHOLDER / N/C and opens its source, method, limits and SHA-256. A value that cannot be computed shows the reason instead of a 0, and slope or roughness hazard flags appear only against thresholds the user enters, so the assumptions stay the user's own.

Tools: Python (FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, NumPy, SciPy, SpiceyPy, rasterio) for the science core, data acquisition and API; PostgreSQL for the site registry; Next.js, React, TanStack Query, Three.js and React Three Fiber for the interface; hosted on Render. Datasets are fetched by manifest with SHA-256 verification. Code: https://github.com/5764678/LUNARSEYE

Use of Super Intelligence (SI): AI coding assistance (Claude, by Anthropic) was used while writing and refactoring the project's code and when drafting this submission text. All scientific methods, data choices and results were checked by the team against the NASA data and the tests in the repository. No images, video or audio were AI-generated, and no NASA branding was used.

Limits: coordinates are DEM tile centres, not landing points; the Moon view is a smooth sphere lit from the computed Sun direction and does not draw terrain shadows (sunlight numbers come only from the timeline); this is a preliminary research tool, not a certified landing system.
dataRefs: LOLA LDEM_75S_240M south-polar DEM (LRO, NASA PDS Geosciences Node)
PGDA LOLA south-pole DEM LDEM_80S_20MPP_ADJ, 20 m/pixel (product 90)
PGDA product 78: LOLA topography for lunar south pole sites (candidate site catalogue)
NAIF SPICE generic kernels (DE440s ephemeris, lunar PCK and frames, leap seconds)
NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit color map (globe texture only; credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio)
projectRefs: Barker et al. (2021), High-resolution LOLA topography for lunar south pole sites, Planetary and Space Science 203, 105119
Next.js and React (web interface framework, open source)
Three.js and React Three Fiber (3D Moon rendering, open source)
FastAPI (Python web API framework, open source)
SpiceyPy (Python wrapper for NASA NAIF SPICE toolkit, open source)
rasterio (GDAL-based raster reading for the LOLA DEMs, open source)
NumPy and SciPy (numerical computing, open source)
Claude by Anthropic (AI coding assistant; see Use of Super Intelligence in Project Details)
